planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: This English lavender selection is prized for its unusually soft, pale pink flower spikes, a rare break from the typical blue-violet lavender palette, held above compact, tidy gray-green foliage. It blooms a bit later than 'Hidcote' or 'Munstead' and holds its color best with some afternoon shade in hot summer climates, since intense heat can wash the pink toward white. Plant in gritty, fast-draining soil and avoid overwatering or rich fertilizer, both of which encourage floppy growth and root rot. Shear lightly after the main flush to maintain a dense mound and encourage a possible rebloom.

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, well-drained, neutral-to-alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: One of the earliest English lavenders to flower each season, this compact heirloom cultivar produces slender, deep violet-blue spikes with an exceptionally sweet, classic lavender scent on narrow silvery foliage. Its early bloom window and neat, rounded habit make it a favorite for edging paths and low hedges, and the flowers dry especially well for sachets and culinary use. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, since wet feet in winter are the most common cause of failure, and shear back by about a third right after flowering to keep the plant compact and woody growth in check.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: A softer-flowered sport of the pink-toned lavender group, this cultivar carries long spikes in a pale lilac-pink wash over compact gray-green foliage, giving a gentler, pastel effect than standard violet-blue English lavenders in mixed borders. It shares the toughness of its species, tolerating heat and drought once established but resenting humid or waterlogged soil. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, avoid heavy mulch against the crown, and shear back after the first flush of bloom to keep growth dense and encourage a second, lighter round of flowers.

planting.note: Transplant nursery starts after all danger of frost into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; in cold climates grow in containers and overwinter under cover.

directions: This Spanish lavender selection produces dense, plump flower cones topped with tall, showy purple bracts that resemble rabbit ears or butterfly wings, blooming earlier and more repeatedly through the season than many other stoechas types on a naturally compact, rounded plant. It is less cold-hardy than English lavenders and struggles in humid summers or heavy soils, so gardeners outside its comfort zone often grow it in pots that can be moved to shelter for winter. Give it full sun, lean soil, and minimal supplemental water once established, and deadhead spent spikes regularly to keep the repeat bloom coming.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps can also be divided in early spring or fall.

directions: A taller, sturdy selection of spike speedwell, this cultivar sends up dense, tapering spires of soft lavender-blue flowers above a low mound of narrow green leaves from early to midsummer, with reliable deadheading extending the show. It is tougher and more heat- and drought-tolerant than it looks, thriving in lean to average garden soil but declining in rich, wet conditions where clumps can flop or rot. Plant in full sun, divide every few years to maintain vigor, and shear back hard after the first bloom flush to encourage a smaller rebloom later in the season.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: One of the most compact and richly colored spike speedwells, this Award of Garden Merit-winning cultivar bears dense, deep rose-pink to magenta flower spikes over a tidy mound of dark green foliage from early to late summer. Its short, sturdy stems rarely need staking, making it a reliable front-of-border choice that pairs well with silver-leaved companions and ornamental grasses. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, deadhead spent spikes to prolong bloom, and divide every two to three years in spring to keep clumps vigorous.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps spread by rosettes and are easily divided.

directions: This early-blooming speedwell forms a low, spreading rosette of glossy, semi-evergreen leaves that sends up loose spikes of pale, almost translucent ice-blue flowers with darker veining in late spring, well ahead of most other speedwells. It is unusually adaptable, tolerating both full sun and light shade and spreading gently by short rhizomes to form a durable groundcover-like clump without becoming invasive. Plant in evenly moist, well-drained soil, shear off spent flower stalks to keep the foliage mat tidy, and divide every three to four years in spring if clumps become congested.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species dislikes wet winter soil more than most other speedwells.

directions: This low, woody-based mat former hugs the ground with small toothed leaves and covers itself in short upright racemes of vivid blue flowers in late spring, making it a classic choice for rock gardens, dry stone walls, and sunny slopes. Unlike shade-loving creeping speedwells, this species wants full sun and lean, fast-draining soil, and it is notably more drought tolerant but far less tolerant of winter wet, which can cause crown rot. Shear the mat lightly after flowering to keep it dense, and divide congested patches in spring every few years to renew vigor.
